keyConcepts.title: Forwarding vs. routing
keyConcepts.text: **Forwarding** (data plane) is router-local: move a packet from an input link to an output link in nanoseconds, in hardware. **Routing** (control plane) computes network-wide paths in seconds, in software.

keyConcepts.title: Best-effort service
keyConcepts.text: IP makes no guarantees about delivery, order, timing or bandwidth. It's simple, and it has worked well with adaptive apps and enough bandwidth.

keyConcepts.title: Inside a router
keyConcepts.text: Input ports (lookup), switching fabric (memory, bus or crossbar), output ports (queuing) and a routing processor (control plane).

keyConcepts.title: Longest prefix matching
keyConcepts.text: Forwarding tables hold address **prefixes**; when several match, the **longest** (most specific) wins. Hardware like TCAMs makes lookups take one clock cycle.

keyConcepts.title: Queuing and scheduling
keyConcepts.text: Queues form at inputs (HOL blocking) and outputs. Scheduling can be FIFO, priority, round robin or **WFQ** (each class gets w_i/Σw_j of the link). Too much buffering causes bufferbloat.

keyConcepts.title: IPv4 datagram and fragmentation
keyConcepts.text: A 20-byte header with TTL, protocol (6 = TCP, 17 = UDP) and checksum. Large datagrams are fragmented to fit smaller MTUs and reassembled only at the destination; offsets are in 8-byte units.

keyConcepts.title: Addressing: subnets and CIDR
keyConcepts.text: Addresses belong to **interfaces**. a.b.c.d/x means the first x bits are the network prefix, which enables route aggregation.

keyConcepts.title: DHCP and NAT
keyConcepts.text: DHCP assigns an IP address, mask, gateway and DNS server (discover, offer, request, ACK). NAT lets many private addresses share one public address using port mappings.

keyConcepts.title: IPv6
keyConcepts.text: 128-bit addresses, a fixed 40-byte header and flow labels. No fragmentation at routers, no header checksum and no options. It's deployed alongside IPv4 using **tunneling**.

keyConcepts.title: Generalized forwarding (SDN/OpenFlow)
keyConcepts.text: Match on many header fields (link, network and transport), then **forward, drop or modify**. One mechanism can act as a router, switch, firewall or NAT.

keyConcepts.title: Middleboxes and architecture
keyConcepts.text: NAT, firewalls, IDS, load balancers and caches sit in the data path. IP is the **narrow waist** of the hourglass, and the **end-to-end argument** keeps smarts at the edges.

options: Moving a packet from a router's input link to the right output link
Computing paths across the whole network
quiz.explain: Forwarding is the local data-plane action. Routing is the network-wide control-plane process.

options: Link 1, because its prefix is longer
Link 2, because it was listed second
quiz.explain: Both prefixes match, but longest prefix matching picks the 24-bit prefix (link 1) over the 21-bit one.

options: A packet at the front of an input queue waiting for a busy output
Output buffers that are too large
quiz.explain: The blocked packet at the front holds up packets behind it, even if their outputs are free.

quiz.q: Under WFQ, three classes have weights 1, 1 and 2 on a 100 Mbps link. What is the minimum rate of the weight-2 class?
quiz.explain: w_i/Σw = 2/4 = 0.5, so it's guaranteed at least 50 Mbps.

quiz.q: What does a router do when a datagram's TTL reaches 0?
quiz.explain: TTL stops datagrams from circulating forever. A dropped datagram triggers an ICMP TTL-expired message.

quiz.q: A 4,000-byte datagram (20-byte header) crosses a link with a 1,500-byte MTU. How many fragments are created?
quiz.explain: 3,980 data bytes split into 1,480 + 1,480 + 1,020, giving 3 fragments with offsets 0, 185 and 370.

quiz.q: How many addresses are in a /24 block?
Which is the correct order of DHCP messages?
quiz.explain: DORA: the client discovers, servers offer, the client requests one offer, and the server ACKs it.

quiz.q: What does a NAT router change in outgoing datagrams?
options: The source IP address and source port
quiz.explain: It replaces the private (IP, port) with its public IP and a new port, and records the mapping in its NAT table.

quiz.q: Which feature is NOT in the IPv6 header?
quiz.explain: IPv6 dropped the header checksum (and router fragmentation and options) to speed up processing.

quiz.q: How do IPv6 datagrams cross a section of IPv4-only routers?
options: Routers translate them to Ethernet frames
quiz.explain: The IPv6 datagram becomes the payload of an IPv4 datagram (protocol 41) until it reaches an IPv6 node.

quiz.q: In OpenFlow, what can a flow table action NOT do?
options: Compute shortest paths across the network
quiz.explain: Switches just match and act. Path computation is done by the SDN controller and its applications.
Middleboxes sit on the data path doing more than routing: NAT, firewalls, IDS, load balancers and caches.
